query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small, tailored concentration of a self-lubricating additive that forms a robust, in‐situ tribo‐film will enable a CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy to maintain low friction and wear rates from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, coarse-grained CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with presently variable tribological performance due to grain coarseness and a propensity for unstable oxide formation at high temperatures.
generation.intervention: Micro-alloying the CoCrFeNi matrix with a small amount of a self-lubricating element (or compound precursor) that is activated by sliding, without predetermining its chemical class, e.g. an additive that can form a lubricious sulfidic or chalcogenide phase.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests performed over a broad temperature range (room temperature to 800 °C) under variable normal loads and in environments that may either promote or limit oxidation (e.g., ambient air and inert gas conditions).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a thin, adherent, nanocrystalline (or amorphous) tribo-film generated through friction-induced activation and element segregation of the additive.
generation.mechanism: During sliding, the additive is activated to form a stable, self-lubricating film on the contact surface. This film mitigates direct metal-to-metal contact and stabilizes the dynamic grain refinement process, countering both the inverse Hall-Petch softening at low loads and the deleterious oxide layer cracking at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated CoCrFeNi alloy, the treated alloy will exhibit a reduced coefficient of friction (targeting values near or below 0.2) and a lower, more consistent wear rate across the full temperature range, even as load and environmental factors vary.
generation.baseline: The performance of the unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, which shows increasing friction and wear variability due to unstable oxide formation and friction-induced grain refinement that is not self-regulated.
generation.boundary: Effectiveness is expected between room temperature and 800 °C. This intervention is designed to be robust under both low and high load conditions and in environments where oxidation can play a role, but not in extreme oxidizing or reducing conditions beyond those tested.
generation.uncertainty: The precise chemical nature and optimal concentration of the additive is uncertain, as is the long-term stability of the friction-induced tribo-film under cyclic loading; further, the interplay between ambient environment and film formation needs to be validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of baseline CoCrFeNi alloy specimens and one set modified with the selected self-lubricating additive at the proposed concentration. Use a controlled pin-on-disk tribometer to perform sliding wear experiments over temperatures ranging from room temperature to 800 °C. Test under multiple normal loads and in both ambient and controlled (e.g., low oxygen) environments. Characterize the wear tracks using interferometry and scanning electron microscopy to assess tribo-film formation, and measure friction coefficients and wear rates throughout the tests.
measurements: Coefficient of friction as a function of temperature and load
Wear rate (volume loss per unit sliding distance and load)
Surface microstructure, with emphasis on the existence and continuity of the tribo-film
Phase or chemical analysis (e.g., EDS or XPS) of the worn surface to confirm the formation of the lubricious phase
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the modified CoCrFeNi alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate across the full temperature range relative to the baseline or if the in-situ tribo-film either does not form or degrades rapidly under conditions expected to activate it.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

In this study, we successfully synthesized a transition metal dichalcogenide high entropy alloy of (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 with 2D structure and tested its tribological properties by performing ball‐on‐disk friction experiments using steel against steel tribopair in an ambient environment. The lubricant was coated onto the steel substrate by the conventional air spray coating process. The lubricant displayed excellent tribological properties with low average coefficient of friction (COF) and wear rates of ≈0.076 and 2.6 × 10−9 mm3 (N∙m)−1, respectively, at the high load of 9 N (contact pressure: 0.936 GPa). The analyses performed on the wear track and wear debris indicate stress‐induced tribocatalytic activity that facilitates the self‐lubricating behavior of HEA nanoflakes during friction tests performed in ambient conditions.

The volume lost was determined using a high-resolution topographical interferometric scan of the entire length of each wear track. In Fig. 3 we show the present results compared to a summary of published steady-state friction coefficients and wear rates for a wide range of high entropy alloys. In the case of multi-phase alloys, these are differentiated as FCC- or BCC-based, corresponding to the primary phase. In all but the present case, the data correspond to experiments performed in environments with sufficient oxygen concentration to drive the formation of mixed metal-oxide films. A conclusion of this work is that, when sheared in UHV, the soft, single-phase (FCC), initially coarse grained (42 µm) CoCrFeMnNi specimens used in this investigation showed nearly the lowest wear rates. This is surprising given that shear deformation of HEAs, even high hardness (BCC) and multi-phase (FCC-BCC) alloys, generally shows rapid formation of mixed metal-oxide surface films that tend to reduce wear rate, and increase hardness.
